Typecho Fans plugins repository distributed a credential-stealing workflow

Target: Typecho Fans plugins · repo
Date: 2026-09-05
Target Kind: project
Language: Shell
Cause: compromised_account_credentials
Impact: credential_theft
Phase: source

Synopsis

A compromised contributor account added a malicious GitHub Actions workflow to Typecho Fans plugins. The workflow attempted to send repository credentials to an attacker-controlled server.

Story

An attacker returned to a compromised community plugin repository in October and tried to restart a secret-stealing workflow without changing the malware. StepSecurity found an empty commit followed by a small README edit in typecho-fans/plugins, both intended to trigger automation already present since September 5. This time, the resulting runs stopped at an approval requirement.

Typecho Fans maintained a collection of plugins for the Typecho blogging platform, with an index and download links for users and a shared repository for contributors. The retained September snapshot contained a workflow called Github Actions Security. Its name suggested maintenance, but the single substantive command sent API_MIRROR, GITEE_TOKEN, and SYNC_PV to an external HTTP endpoint. Those secret references tied the payload to the repository's automation rather than to a particular blog plugin's PHP code.

The workflow supported both push events and manual dispatch. Its preceding cache-busting step only wrote a timestamp into the job environment; the next step attempted the secret transfer. The October edits therefore did not need to add another loader or modify a plugin to create a new execution opportunity. StepSecurity associated the activity with the compromised xxyangyoulin account and documented the October 7 runs remaining in action_required.

That approval gate prevented the observed October attempts from executing, but it did not establish that the earlier September workflow had never run. The preserved source proved an upstream CI implant, not poisoned plugin archives or infection of Typecho websites. OpenSourceMalware's GhostAction research corroborated the wider campaign's use of such workflows; the outcome for any earlier secrets exposed from this particular repository remained unconfirmed.
